Retaining Wall Brisbane Options, Material By Material Material is usually the first thing people try to decide and the last thing that should be locked in. Height, surcharge and drainage set the engineering; the material then follows from the site, the access and the budget. Concrete sleeper walls, steel-reinforced planks slotted between galvanised posts, do most of the work on Brisbane cut-and-fill blocks. Timber sleeper walls still suit low garden terraces. Core-filled block carries taller engineered loads and takes a render. Sandstone, boulder and gabion walls sit better on larger, steeper sites and drain freely by nature. Behind every one of them, subsoil drainage is the part that decides whether the wall is still straight in fifteen years. Concrete Sleeper Retaining Walls Steel-reinforced concrete sleepers set between galvanised H-posts - the workhorse wall for Brisbane's cut-and-fill blocks and the usual replacement when a timber wall gives out. View service -> When a wall needs building approval in Queensland The familiar shorthand, "over a metre needs council approval", is only the first of five conditions. Under the Building Regulation 2021 and the Queensland Development Code, a wall avoids building approval only if it clears every one of the following. Brisbane City Council sets the same triggers out on its retaining wall page . 1 Total height over 1.0 metre Measured on the wall plus any retained fill or cut above natural ground level, not just the visible face. 2 Any surcharge load, at any height A driveway, building, pool or second wall sitting in the zone of influence behind the wall counts, even on a low wall. 3 Within 1.5 metres of a structure Close to a house, shed or another retaining wall, the two structures start to interact and approval applies. 4 Part of a pool barrier Where the wall forms part of the pool fence line, it is assessed as part of the barrier. 5 Wall plus fence 2.0 metres or more A modest wall with a fence on top can reach the combined-height trigger without either part looking tall. Approval and licensing are separate questions. Building approval turns on those physical triggers; QBCC licensing turns on the dollar value of the work. A low wall that needs no approval can still need a licensed contractor. Where approval does apply, the wall is generally designed to AS 4678 by an RPEQ engineer and certified on a Form 15. More detail sits on the engineered and council-approved walls page. Why one quote is double the other Retaining walls are priced on the face area of the wall, height times length, not on lineal metres.
